Detection of Potato Plant Leaf Diseases using

Convolutional Neural Networks

Haimanot Bitew Alemayehu1, Simachew Melaku Ayalew2,

Chilotie Desalew Mengesha3, Ayisheshim Almaw Bogale4

, Anteneh Birhan Yenew5, Abrham Tegegne Bogale6

6,5,4,3,2,1College of Engineering & Technology, Injibara University, Ethiopia
1haimanot.bitew@inu.edu.et, 2simachew.melaku@inu.edu.et
3chilotie.dessalew@inu.edu.et, 4ayisheshim.almaw@inu.edu.et
5anteneh.birhan@inu.edu.et, 6abrham.tegegne@inu.edu.et

October 15, 2026

Abstract

Potato is a food-security crop in Ethiopia but production is affected by foliar diseases, es-
pecially early blight and late blight. In farming areas disease identification still depends on
visual assessment or laboratory diagnosis approaches that can be slow or difficult to access.
This study develops a convolutional neural network (CNN) for recognizing three potato leaf
conditions: healthy leaves, early blight and late blight. The proposed model was trained us-
ing 2,215 images from PlantVillage. Subsequently assessed with an independent field dataset
containing 247 images collected from potato farms in Banja Awi Zone, Ethiopia. On PlantVil-
lage the model obtained 99.04% training accuracy, 98.21% validation accuracy and 98.66%
test accuracy. On the field dataset, which represents controlled image-capture conditions
the model achieved 90.28% accuracy. The study also compares the proposed network with
VGG16.
Mobilenetv2 using classification performance and computational characteristics.
The proposed model contains 446,787 parameters and has an approximate size of 1.70 MB.
The model’s training time was shorter, than the training time of VGG16 and MobileNetV2.
These results indicate that a compact CNN can provide potato disease classification while re-
ducing computational requirements with potential to benefit smallholder farmers in Ethiopia
and similar agricultural contexts.

Keywords: Potato leaf disease, neural network, Deep learning, Late blight, Early blight

1
Introduction

Agriculture is a part of food production and livelihoods in Ethiopia and potato is one of the im-
portant root and tuber crops grown in the country. Potato production however faces constraints,
including foliar diseases. Early blight, caused by Alternaria solani and late blight, caused by
Phytophthora infestans are especially important because infections can reduce crop productiv-
ity. Previous work in Awi Zone has also reported the presence of late blight in potato-growing
districts [1].

In farming communities people identify potato disease by looking at the leaves. Laboratory
tests can give proof but are not always easy to get. Image-based automated classification can
give preliminary identification from leaf images.

Another challenge is that early and late blight symptoms look similar especially as they
develop. This similarity makes it hard to tell them apart. Can influence disease management
decisions [2].

1

CNNs are widely used for image-based plant disease recognition because the convolutional
layers can learn patterns directly from training images. Researchers have used them for crops
and disease types including potato leaf conditions [3].

For potato disease classification Mahapatra and Panda achieved 96.28% accuracy with a
CNN on PlantVillage data [3]. Hoque et al. Achieved 99.14% accuracy with a lightweight CNN
[4]. Dey et al. Described a CNN with 204,227 trainable parameters and reported 98.6% test
accuracy [5].

These results show the potential of CNNs Performance on controlled image sets does not
always match performance on field images.
This difference motivates testing with collected
images along with benchmark data. This study focuses on a CNN that classifies three classes
healthy, early blight and late blight paying close attention to computational efficiency and testing
in local field conditions.

The study notice that many existing potato-disease studies have limitations. They often
use datasets with uniform backgrounds and lighting. These conditions make classification easier
than when photos have varying light, background, leaf angle and symptom appearance. Also
evidence specific to potato disease in farms is limited.

So the study. Tested a lightweight CNN that recognizes the three chosen potato leaf condi-
tions and looked at how the model behaves on a benchmark dataset and on images taken from
farms in Awi Zone.

2
Related Works

The study have seen that recent research focuses more on learning for plant disease recognition.
In a review Pacal et al. Covered many studies on deep-learning methods for plant diseases and
highlighted CNNs as a main way to classify images [7]. CNNs are useful because they learn
feature representations from images during training of needing all visual descriptors to be made
manually [8].

2.1
CNN-Based Approaches for Potato Disease Identification

The study see that studies on potato leaf classification have used custom CNNs and transfer-learning
models. Mahapatra and Panda got 96.28 achieved accuracy using a CNN on PlantVillage im-
ages [3]. Hoque et al. Got 99.14 achieved accuracy using a CNN and included regularization
techniques, like dropout and batch normalization [4]. Dey et al. Created a CNN with 204,227
parameters and said the test accuracy was 98.6 percent [5].

Mulugeta et al. Evaluated a CNN on PlantVillage images and field samples from Ethiopia.
Their study reported 85% accuracy 87% precision, 85% recall and 86% F1-score on the data [6].
These results show the performance gap that can happen when a model shifts, from controlled

benchmark images to field observations.

2.2
Transfer Learning in Potato Leaf Disease Classification

Transfer learning is an used strategy for plant disease recognition. Architectures such as VGG16,
MobileNetV2, ResNet50 InceptionV3 and DenseNet121 have been employed in image classifi-
cation studies [9]. Ensemble methods have also merged pretrained networks [10]. Pretrained
models can provide feature representations but their parameter counts and computational sig-
nificantly vary a lot. This difference matters a lot when running them on hardware, with power.
Transfer learning stays important because it helps balance how well a model performs with how
resources it uses.

2

2.3
Real-World Application of CNN Models

A frequent concern in plant-disease classification is whether high benchmark accuracy can trans-
fer to images taken in farm settings. Studies that use PlantVillage-style images might benefit
from controlled capture conditions. For instance KWATCHNet reportedly achieved 99.81% on
PlantVillage data and 93.34% on field-collected images [12]. This difference shows why an inde-
pendent field dataset is valuable when testing generalization. Plant-disease classification must
therefore be validated in real-world scenarios.

Research on potato disease recognition in Ethiopia is still growing. Existing studies have
explored CNN architectures and the classification of blight symptoms [13]. Further investigation
that uses collected images and computationally efficient models can help determine how well
automated approaches work under regional farming conditions [14].

3
Methodology

An experimental design was used to develop, train and evaluate the proposed CNN. The experi-
mental procedure involved dataset preparation, image preprocessing and augmentation network
construction, model training, performance measurement and comparison with transfer-learning
baselines. Both benchmark images and collected field images were included. The methodology
covers dataset collection and preprocessing, model architecture design, training and hyperpa-
rameter optimization and thorough evaluation using both benchmark and collected datasets.

3.1
Dataset

The main training and initial evaluation dataset includes 2,215 potato leaf images taken from
PlantVillage [15]. These images belong to three classes: early blight and late blight. PlantVil-
lage images were captured under controlled conditions with consistent lighting and uniform
background.

3.2
Field Validation Dataset

To assess performance under farm conditions 247 extra potato leaf photographs were collected
from farms in Banja district Awi Zone, Ethiopia [16].
These photographs were taken with
smartphones in light. The images belong to the three target classes and their labels were verified
by an agricultural extension expert. The field dataset was kept apart, from model training and
validation. Was used for final field testing.

3.3
Data Preprocessing

Preprocessing was applied to make the images consistent with the CNN input requirements and
to support stable model training. The same general preprocessing procedure was used for the
benchmark and field images.

• Image resizing: each photograph was converted to the fixed spatial dimensions required
by the network.

• Pixel normalization: image intensity values were transformed to the interval [0, 1] before
being supplied to the model.

• Data augmentation: training images were varied using operations such as rotation, hor-
izontal reflection, zooming, and brightness modification [17]. These transformations were
intended to expose the model to greater visual variation during learning.

3

3.4
Proposed CNN Architecture

The proposed CNN was designed with a focus on a balance between classification performance
and computational cost. Its relatively small parameter count was intended to make subsequent
edge-oriented deployment more practical.

Figure 1: Proposed CNN Architecture

The architecture contains approximately 446,787 trainable parameters and occupies about
1.70 MB.These characteristics make the proposed network substantially smaller than the com-
pared transfer-learning configurations [18], while maintaining a lightweight architecture.

4
Results

4.1
Model Training Performance

During training on PlantVillage, the accuracy curves showed convergence of the model on the
training and validation data.
Training accuracy reached 99.04%, while validation accuracy
reached 98.21%. The reported validation loss at the end of training was 0.0833.

4.2
Model Test Performance on PlantVillage

Evaluation on the held-out PlantVillage test set produced an overall accuracy of 98.66%. The
confusion matrix (Table 1) indicates that most samples were assigned to their correct classes,
with a small number of errors distributed among the three categories.

This is

ways symptoms appeared. The model achieved 90.28% accuracy and a loss of 0.4615 on these

CNN was evaluated alongside VGG16 and MobileNetV2 after the comparison models had been

The accuracy difference between the PlantVillage test evaluation and the field evaluation is
8.38 percentage points for the proposed model. This accuracy difference shows that the field
evaluation images are harder to classify than the controlled benchmark images and gives a
measure of the proposed models performance, across different settings.

4.5
Training Efficiency

The proposed model took 5.58 seconds per epoch in the comparison. VGG16 took 9.96 seconds.
Mobilenetv2 took 7.68 seconds. Therefore within the setup the proposed network needed less
training time than both comparison configurations.

5
Discussion

The paper found that the proposed lightweight CNN successfully completed the goal of detecting
potato leaf disease. The model performed well on both the PlantVillage dataset and on the field
collected dataset.

In the reported experiments the proposed network reached 99.04% training accuracy, 98.21%
validation accuracy and 98.66% PlantVillage test accuracy. The field evaluation yielded 90.28%

7

accuracy. The comparison tables show that the proposed configuration had a validation loss
than VGG16 and MobileNetV2 in the same experiment.

The gap between training and validation accuracy was small during the reported training
run. Yet the performance on the independent field dataset was lower than on PlantVillage. This
difference matches the visual variability that comes from field image capture and it shows that
benchmark performance should not be taken as the same as field performance.

The paper observed that the proposed architecture has 446,787 parameters and a size of about
1.70 MB. Its epoch time was 5.58 seconds while VGG16 took 9.96 seconds. Mobilenetv2 took
7.68 seconds. These measurements confirm that the proposed architecture is computationally
compact in the reported environment.

The paper noted that a compact model can be helpful where computing resources or con-
nectivity are limited. In the field experiment the proposed model achieved 90.28% accuracy.
Mulugeta et al. Reported accuracy, on their collected Ethiopian dataset. Because these accu-
racy results come from datasets and experimental settings results should be seen as findings,
not a direct comparison.

6
Conclusion

This study developed and evaluated a lightweight CNN for classification of potato leaves into
healthy, early blight, and late blight categories. The proposed model achieved 98.66% test accu-
racy on the selected PlantVillage test set and 90.28% accuracy on the independently collected
Banja field dataset. The comparison experiments also examined VGG16 and MobileNetV2 in
terms of performance and computational characteristics.

The main contributions of the present study are as follows:

1. Proposing an automated system for the detection of potato leaf diseases using a lightweight
CNN.

2. The proposed configuration recorded 98.66% PlantVillage test accuracy, while the com-
parative experiment reports a 0.0268 validation loss for the proposed model. These results
describe the performance of the proposed configuration under the stated experimental setup.

3. On the Banja field dataset, the proposed model obtained 90.28% accuracy. The difference
between the PlantVillage test accuracy and the field accuracy was 8.38 percentage points
when those two test results are compared directly.

4. The model contains 446,787 trainable parameters and has an approximate size of 1.70 MB.
The reported training-time measurements also indicate a lower average epoch time than the
VGG16 and MobileNetV2 configurations used for comparison.

The findings indicate that lightweight image-classification models may have practical rele-
vance to precision-agriculture applications. A field-deployed system could provide preliminary
disease classification from leaf photographs, although operational treatment decisions should
remain supported by appropriate agricultural expertise.

The results indicate potential for further investigation of deep-learning-based potato disease
management in Awi Zone. Future work will focus on:

• Increasing the number of Banja field images used for future fine-tuning and evaluation.

• Extending the class set to include additional potato diseases, including bacterial wilt and
virus-related symptoms, as well as healthy leaves affected by non-disease stress.

• Developing a mobile application with a simple user interface and local-language support,
including Amharic and Awign.

• Combining image-based diagnosis with weather information to investigate an early-warning
framework for disease risk.

8

• Assessing the practical and economic effects of the system through field-based evaluation
with farmers.

potato leaf disease. The model performed well on both the PlantVillage dataset and on the field
collected dataset.

In the reported experiments the proposed network reached 99.04% training accuracy, 98.21%
validation accuracy and 98.66% PlantVillage test accuracy. The field evaluation yielded 90.28%

accuracy. The comparison tables show that the proposed configuration had a validation loss
than VGG16 and MobileNetV2 in the same experiment.

The gap between training and validation accuracy was small during the reported training
run. Yet the performance on the independent field dataset was lower than on PlantVillage. This
difference matches the visual variability that comes from field image capture and it shows that
benchmark performance should not be taken as the same as field performance.

The paper observed that the proposed architecture has 446,787 parameters and a size of about
1.70 MB. Its epoch time was 5.58 seconds while VGG16 took 9.96 seconds. Mobilenetv2 took
7.68 seconds. These measurements confirm that the proposed architecture is computationally
compact in the reported environment.

The paper noted that a compact model can be helpful where computing resources or con-
nectivity are limited. In the field experiment the proposed model achieved 90.28% accuracy.
Mulugeta et al. Reported accuracy, on their collected Ethiopian dataset. Because these accu-
racy results come from datasets and experimental settings results should be seen as findings,
not a direct comparison.

Conclusion

This study developed and evaluated a lightweight CNN for classification of potato leaves into
healthy, early blight, and late blight categories. The proposed model achieved 98.66% test accu-
racy on the selected PlantVillage test set and 90.28% accuracy on the independently collected
Banja field dataset. The comparison experiments also examined VGG16 and MobileNetV2 in
terms of performance and computational characteristics.
The main contributions of the present study are as follows:

1. Proposing an automated system for the detection of potato leaf diseases using a lightweight
CNN.

2. The proposed configuration recorded 98.66% PlantVillage test accuracy, while the com-
parative experiment reports a 0.0268 validation loss for the proposed model. These results
describe the performance of the proposed configuration under the stated experimental setup.

3. On the Banja field dataset, the proposed model obtained 90.28% accuracy. The difference
between the PlantVillage test accuracy and the field accuracy was 8.38 percentage points
when those two test results are compared directly.

4. The model contains 446,787 trainable parameters and has an approximate size of 1.70 MB.
The reported training-time measurements also indicate a lower average epoch time than the
VGG16 and MobileNetV2 configurations used for comparison.

The findings indicate that lightweight image-classification models may have practical rele-
vance to precision-agriculture applications. A field-deployed system could provide preliminary
disease classification from leaf photographs, although operational treatment decisions should
remain supported by appropriate agricultural expertise.

The results indicate potential for further investigation of deep-learning-based potato disease
management in Awi Zone. Future work will focus on:
• Increasing the number of Banja field images used for future fine-tuning and evaluation.

• Extending the class set to include additional potato diseases, including bacterial wilt and
virus-related symptoms, as well as healthy leaves affected by non-disease stress.

• Developing a mobile application with a simple user interface and local-language support,
including Amharic and Awign.

• Combining image-based diagnosis with weather information to investigate an early-warning
framework for disease risk.

• Assessing the practical and economic effects of the system through field-based evaluation
with farmers.
